lawyer:
Md. Shahjahan ------- For the Petitioners.
Md. Ansar Ali ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Osir Uddin Mandal and ors ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Azizur Rahman ------ Opp. Party.
full_judgment:
1. This Rule seeks to call in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 19.12.80 passed by Subordinate Judge, Bogra in Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979. 

 2. Facts giving rise to this application may briefly be stated thus. The petitioners figuring as plaintiffs instituted a partition suit being T.S. No. 60 of 1960 in, the court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra in which opposite-party Azizur Rahman Pramanik figured as defendant No. 20. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on contest against all except defendant No. 20 against whom an ex-parte decree was passed. Being aggrieved by ex-parte dceree opposite-party (defendant) Azizur Rahman Pramanik filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979 in which petitioners were impleaded as opposite party. Opposite-party Azizur Rahman sought to have preliminary decree set aside on the ground that summons was not served on him and that it was suppressed in collusion with the process server. Learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence and other the materials on record held that summons on opposite party Azizur Rahman Pramanik who figured as defendant No. 20 in the original partition suit was not served and on this finding he allowed the application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and had set aside the preliminary decree. Petitioners being aggrieved by the order allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 122 of 1979 moved revisional jurisdiction of this court by filing an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule. 

 3. It appears from the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge that the summons meant for defendant-opposite party Azizur Rahman Pramanik (Defendant No. 20 in the original suit) was received by defendant No. 19 Kasimuddin Pramanik on behalf of defendant No. 20. But no evidence was led, to prove defendant 19 Kasimuddin to be the authorised agent of the opposite party defendant No. 20 and so the learned Subordinate Judge held that Kasimuddin (defendant No. 19) being not an authorised agent of defendant No. 20 defendant No. 20 was not competent to receive summons on behalf of opposite-party defendant No. 20 and on that ground learned Subordinate Judge held that service of summons on opposite party was not effected in accordance with law and on that finding he allowed the miscellaneous case and set aside the ex-parte preliminary decree passed in the original suit against opposite party Azizur Rahman. 

 4. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that though evidence showing Kasimuddin (Defendant No.19) as an authorised agent of defendant opposite party is lacking, this service can be deemed to be proper and valid service in view of the fact that Kasimuddin who received the summons on behalf of opposite-party happens to be the adult male member of his family. In order to support this contention reliance has been placed on the provision laid down under Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which speaks that service effected on adult member of defendant's family in absence of defendant from his residence when the service of summons sought to be effected such service shall be deemed to have been effected properly. It is further argued by the learned counsel that defendant No. 19 who received summons meant for defendant-opposite party, happens to be the adult member of the same family and as such the provision of Order 5, rule 15 is attracted to the facts of this case. 

 5. In repelling the contention urged by the learned counsel for the petitioner, it is submitted by the learned counsel for opposite party that provision contained in Order 5, rule 13 can not have any application to the facts of the case inasmuch as there is no evidence whatsoever to show that Kasimuddin was the adult member of opposite party’s family. It is further urged that summons meant for opposite party was served on Kasimuddin allegedly treating him to be adult male member of opposite party's family during absence of opposite party from his residence, but no evidence has been led to substantiate this plea. To prove this plea best evidence would have been that of process-server concerned but he has not been examined in this case as witness. Thus in absence of any witness supporting service of summons in the manner alleged, aid of Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked. No such plea was set up in the written objection filed in the original miscellaneous case and that ends of justice demands strict proof of service of summons in accordance with law. In support of this contention learned counsel relied on the decision reported in 36 D.L.R. 260. This decision lends unqualified support to his contention and I fully agree with the principle enunciated by his Lordship in the said decision. In elaborating his argument the learned counsel submitted that service of summons on a brother in absence of another brother will not be deemed to be a proper service unless it is proved affirmatively that brother on whom service is effected is authorised agent of the absentee brother. In order to back this contention decision reported In 21 D.L.R. 747 has been referred and relied upon. The learned counsel continued to urge that the expression "family" occurring in rule 15, Order 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure connotes parents and their children and no adult members of the family. To support this contention the decision in the case of Amin Khan Vs. University of Sind reported in P L.D. 899 has been relied upon. 

 6. Heard the learned counsel of both the sides and perused the judgment pronounced by the trial court. I am of opinion that the contention urged by the learned counsel for the opposite party has much substance in it. Nowhere within four corners of written objection filed in the miscellaneous case, it has been asserted that Kasimuddin who received summons meant for opposite party defendant No. 20 is the adult member of the opposite party's family. Farther, the process server who effected service has not been examined in this case to prove that he treated defendant No.19 Kasimuddin to be the adult family member of opposite party defendant No. 20 and accordingly effected the service of summons on him, nor there Is any evidence to prove that Kasimuddin was the authorised agent of defendant No. 20 (opposite party). 

 9. Since it has been found that provision contained in Order 5, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no application to the facts and circumstances of the case, no relief can be claimed by the petitioner relying on that provision. The learned counsel for the petitioner in the last resort submitted that petitioners who figured as opposite party in the original miscellaneous case did not get a chance to contest it because of the fact that their senior lawyer being engaged elsewhere did not appear and produce any evidence. But the trial court in his judgment did not mention anything about this matter. Be that as it may, consideration of the matter on compassionate ground cannot be allowed to supersede the mandatory provision of law. Law in this regard enjoins that service of summons on defendant is to be proved strictly according to law and if proof is lacking in this regard mercy or plea of ends of justice cannot come in rescue of the aggrieved party. 

 10. Thus having considered materials on record and regard being had to the facts, circumstances and legal and factual aspects of the matter I am of the opinion that learned Subordinate Judge held correctly that summons in this case was not served upon defendant opposite party in accordance with law and as such no interference in the matter is called for.
